content: Pain during the injection of propofol is a common and undesirable side effect that can negatively impact patient satisfaction. Intravenous administration of lidocaine has been widely used to mitigate this pain. While numerous studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of lidocaine in reducing both the frequency and severity of pain, no prior systematic review has specifically focused on its role in preventing high-intensity pain during propofol injection. The purpose of this review was to evaluate the efficacy and potential adverse effects of lidocaine in preventing high-intensity pain associated with propofol injection. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), Ovid MEDLINE, Ovid Embase, and LILACS, covering studies up to October 2014. An additional search was performed in November 2015, identifying 11 studies awaiting classification, which will be incorporated into future updates of the review. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that investigated the use of intravenous lidocaine to reduce pain during propofol injection in adult patients. Studies without a placebo or control group were excluded. Data from the selected studies were analyzed, and the risk of bias was assessed across five domains: random sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding, completeness of outcome data, and selective reporting. Meta-analyses were conducted using the Mantel-Haenszel method with random effects, and statistical heterogeneity was evaluated using the I² statistic. The overall quality of evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach. A total of 85 studies were included in the review, with 82 studies (involving 10,350 participants) eligible for quantitative analysis. Participants ranged in age from 13 to 89 years and were classified as American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) I-III patients undergoing elective surgery. The studies were conducted in single centers across high-, middle-, and low-income countries. Based on the risk of bias assessment, 77 studies were deemed to have satisfactory methodological quality, while five studies were identified as having a high risk of bias due to issues such as inadequate blinding, incomplete outcome data, or other potential sources of bias. In the control group, the overall incidence of pain during propofol injection was 63.7% (95% CI 60% to 67.9%), with high-intensity pain occurring in 37.9% (95% CI 33.4% to 43.1%) of cases. In contrast, the lidocaine group demonstrated significantly lower rates of pain, with an overall incidence of 30.2% (95% CI 26.7% to 33.7%) and high-intensity pain occurring in only 11.8% (95% CI 9.7% to 13.8%). Both lidocaine admixture (mixing lidocaine with propofol) and lidocaine pretreatment (administering lidocaine prior to propofol injection) were found to be highly effective in reducing pain. Specifically, lidocaine admixture reduced the odds of pain with an odds ratio (OR) of 0.19 (95% CI 0.15 to 0.25) based on 31 studies involving 4,927 participants, while lidocaine pretreatment had an OR of 0.13 (95% CI 0.10 to 0.18) based on 41 RCTs involving 3,918 participants. Both techniques were supported by high-quality evidence. When lidocaine was premixed with propofol, the odds of pain were reduced with an OR of 0.19 (95% CI 0.15 to 0.24) based on 36 studies involving 5,628 participants. Similarly, when lidocaine was administered as a pretreatment, the odds of pain were reduced with an OR of 0.14 (95% CI 0.11 to 0.18) based on 50 studies involving 4,722 participants. These findings were also supported by high-quality evidence. Adverse effects associated with lidocaine administration were rare. Thrombophlebitis was reported in only two studies, but the evidence for this outcome was of low quality, and no odds ratio was estimated. None of the included studies reported data on patient satisfaction. In conclusion, the evidence from currently available RCTs is of high quality and confirms that both lidocaine admixture and pretreatment are effective in reducing pain during propofol injection. There were no significant differences in efficacy between the two techniques.
